question: A team drafts a long monthly report in Claude and keeps exhausting its usage allowance before the month ends. Some sections are routine - recurring summaries and figures pulled from the same sources each time - while other sections carry the analysis the report is read for. The team already signs the report off against an agreed quality checklist, and it wants to cut usage by moving some of the drafting to a lighter Claude model tier without weakening the sections that matter. Which sequence of steps should the team follow?
options: A) Run the routine sections on a lighter tier; decide which sections need human judgment; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
B) Decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
C) Decide which sections need human judgment; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short; run the routine sections on a lighter tier.
D) Check the drafts against the agreed checklist; decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
correct_answers: B) Decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
explanations: Incorrect. The routine sections are moved to the lighter tier before anyone has worked out which sections carry the judgment, so the split is guesswork about the content rather than a decision based on it, and the checklist pass that follows can only repair a division that was arbitrary to start with.

Correct. Deciding which sections need human judgment comes first because it is the only step that reasons about the content rather than the tooling; the lighter tier is then applied only where quality is not at stake; and the checklist the team already signs the report off against is what tells them which moves to keep and which to send back to the deeper tier. Claude Academy's model-selection tutorial applies the same test - run the work on the lighter model, then judge whether the output met your bar.

Incorrect. The drafts are checked and sections are sent back to the deeper tier before the lighter tier has been used at all, so the move to the lighter tier is the last thing done and nothing verifies its output - the one step the team cannot afford to leave unchecked given that quality is the stated constraint.

Incorrect. The checklist pass happens before anything has been moved, so it measures the drafts the team already produces and says nothing about how the lighter tier performs; the final step then sends back sections that were never re-checked after the change.
